dataset.what_one_row_represents: summary.csv: one country radio station's full-year (19-day sample) airplay totals; daySummary.csv: one station-day; pvals.csv: one station's coin-flip p-value
dataset.geographic_scope: 29 stations in 16 U.S. metropolitan markets (Austin, Charlotte, Chicago, Cincinnati, Columbus, Dallas, Greensboro, Houston, Indianapolis, Kansas City, Los Angeles, Nashville, Philadelphia, San Antonio, Tampa, Washington DC)

ana_01.label: 0.5% — back-to-back women vs 65% back-to-back men
ana_01.content: Across 182,848 song plays on 29 country radio stations in 2022, only 928 plays (0.51%) were a song by a women artist immediately following another song by a women artist. Plays where a man's song followed another man's song accounted for 118,861 plays — 65.01% of all airtime. The mean station-level rate was 0.50% women back-to-back vs 65.05% men back-to-back. Among all back-to-back pairs in the dataset (women+men+mixed combined = 120,646), women-on-women pairs are 0.77% and men-on-men pairs are 98.52%. The men-to-women back-to-back ratio is 128:1.

calculation.output:
Total songs: 182,848
b2b women count: 928
b2b men count: 118,861
b2b women % of all songs: 0.51%
b2b men % of all songs: 65.01%
ratio men:women in b2b: 128.1x
mean station b2b women %: 0.50%
mean station b2b men %: 65.05%

data_table.description: Back-to-back play counts and shares of total airtime, by gender bucket

ana_02.label: Airplay share by gender: 81% men, 10% women
ana_02.content: Of every song played, men's songs receive 81.53% of airtime (149,068 plays), women's songs receive 10.07% (18,412 plays), and mixed-gender ensembles receive 8.40% (15,364 plays). Even before considering pairings, the airplay pool is already lopsided 8-to-1 in favour of men.

calculation.output:
women airplay share: 10.07%
men airplay share: 81.53%
mixed airplay share: 8.40%
women count: 18,412
men count: 149,068
mixed count: 15,364

data_table.description: Share of total song plays by artist gender

ana_03.label: Station ranking — KKGO-LA at top, WUBE-Cincinnati at bottom
ana_03.content: Station-level back-to-back women percentages span a 39-fold range. Mount Wilson's KKGO-FM in Los Angeles tops the list at 1.27% (81 b2b-women plays out of 6,380 songs). At the bottom, Cincinnati's Hubbard-owned WUBE-FM has just 0.03% (2 b2b-women plays in 6,221 songs). Only 6 of 29 stations exceed 1%; 17 of 29 are below 0.5%. The median station's b2b-women rate is 0.42%.

calculation.output: BEST: LosAngeles KKGO-FM 1.27% (81/6380); WORST: Cincinnati WUBE-FM 0.03% (2/6221)

data_table.description: All 29 stations ranked by b2b-women percentage

notable_instance.name: Cincinnati WUBE-FM
notable_instance.why: The single most extreme floor: in essentially an entire year of sampled airplay, this Hubbard station paired women back-to-back exactly twice.

ana_04.label: Daypart exile: women's b2b clusters in overnight & evening
ana_04.content: Of the 928 back-to-back women plays, 42.6% (395) occur during the overnight block (12am–6am OVN) and 20.8% (193) during the evening (7pm–12am EVE) — 63.4% of all women's b2b moments happen when audiences are smallest. The two prime drive-time blocks together (AM-Drive 6–10am: 15.3%, PM-Drive 3–7pm: 9.3%) account for only 24.6%. The mid-day block contributes 12.1%. The 'tomato' is being served when the kitchen is empty.

data_table.description: Distribution of women's back-to-back plays across radio dayparts

ana_05.label: Owner-level concentration — small owners outperform iHeart & Cumulus
ana_05.content: Aggregating by station-owner: independent and small operators play women back-to-back more often than the major consolidators. Mount Wilson FM (single station, KKGO-LA) leads at 1.27% b2b-women, followed by Cox (1 station, 0.99%) and COX (1 station, 0.71%). The two largest country owners — iHeartMedia (8 stations) and Cumulus (5 stations) — sit near the bottom of the owner-weighted ranking at 0.40% each, despite controlling 13 of the 29 stations in the dataset. Hubbard (2 stations, 0.12%) and Steel City (2 stations, 0.27%) rank lowest of all.

calculation.output: Hubbard 0.12%, Steel City 0.27%, Cumulus 0.40%, iHeart 0.40%, Emmis 0.47%, Beasley 0.63%, Audacy 0.66%, COX 0.71%, Cox 0.99%, Mount Wilson 1.27%

ana_06.label: Statistical significance — 25 of 29 stations under-pair women below chance
ana_06.content: Using the project's coin-flip simulation (1,000 random shuffles per station-day, holding gender mix constant), 25 of 29 stations have an observed b2b-women rate that falls below chance at p < 0.05; 18 stations have p = 0 (observed below ALL 1,000 simulations) — meaning under random scheduling the actual women-pairing count is essentially impossible. Only 4 stations (KAJA-SA, WUSN-Chicago, KASE-Austin, WTQR-Greensboro) fail to reach significance. This is empirical evidence the under-pairing is structural — programmed in — not random.

calculation.output:
Stations with p<0.05 for women under-pairing: 25 / 29
Stations with p==0: 18
(See full p-value table)

data_table.description: Coin-flip simulation p-values for under-pairing of women per station (lower = more anomalous)

ana_07.label: Catalogue tilt — women's b2b leans on legacy hits, not new releases
ana_07.content: When women are paired back-to-back, the songs are most often older. Of 928 women-b2b plays, 415 (44.7%) are recurrent songs (recent but past peak), 309 (33.3%) are gold (older catalog hits), and only 204 (22.0%) are current releases. So for every back-to-back pair of brand-new women's songs, there are ~3.5 pairs of older women's hits. Stations are willing to play women together — when those women are Reba McEntire or Shania Twain, not a debut artist.

data_table.description: Women's back-to-back plays by song-age category

ana_08.label: Women of color: 0.015% of plays, 0 back-to-back
ana_08.content: Of 182,848 plays, women of color account for 27 plays — 0.015% of all airtime. Across the entire dataset, there are zero back-to-back plays of women-of-color artists. White women account for 99.85% of women's airplay; women of color account for 0.15%. By contrast, men of color get 6.57% of plays and account for 695 back-to-back men-of-color pairs (0.38% of total plays). The most under-represented intersection on country radio is therefore not women, and not artists of color, but the overlap: women of color, who appear roughly once per 7,000 plays.

calculation.output:
POC women airplay: 27 (0.0148%)
b2b POC women: 0 (0.0000%)
white women / all women airplay: 99.85%
POC women / all women airplay: 0.15%

data_table.description: Airplay & back-to-back counts at the intersection of gender and race

ana_09.label: Day-to-day variance — best day still under 1% women back-to-back
ana_09.content: Even on the strongest sampled day across all 29 stations (April 8, 2022, the release date of several women's singles), the cross-station mean back-to-back women rate was 0.72%. The weakest sampled day (August 26, 2022) averaged 0.25%. The all-day, all-station spread of station-day b2b-women percentages ranges from 0.00% (many station-days) to a single-day peak of 2.34% (one station on June 13). The median station-day rate is 0.30%. No matter which day you pick, women are virtually never paired together.

calculation.output: Best day mean: 0.72% on 4/8/22; Worst day mean: 0.25% on 8/26/22; daily means range 0.25%–0.72%

data_table.description: Cross-station mean b2b-women % per sampled date

ana_10.label: Best vs worst — 39× spread between KKGO-LA and WUBE-Cincinnati
ana_10.content: The single best station — Mount Wilson's KKGO-FM in Los Angeles — plays women back-to-back at 1.27% (81 b2b plays in 6,380 songs). The single worst — Hubbard's WUBE-FM in Cincinnati — plays women back-to-back at 0.03% (just 2 b2b plays in 6,221 songs). That is a 39× gap between identical-format stations in the same year. Both are mainstream country reporters; both serve large markets; what differs is who programs them.

calculation.output:
BEST b2b-women: LosAngeles KKGO-FM (Mount Wilson FM) 1.27%
WORST b2b-women: Cincinnati WUBE-FM (Hubbard) 0.0321%
Ratio: 39x

data_table.description: Top-3 vs bottom-3 stations on b2b-women rate

ana_11.label: The b2b gap — men minus women per station, mean 64.5 percentage points
ana_11.content: Subtracting each station's b2b-women percentage from its b2b-men percentage produces the simplest measure of the airwave asymmetry. The mean gap is 64.55 percentage points, ranging from a minimum of 58.16 (Mount Wilson KKGO-LA) to a maximum of 73.44 (Steel City KFKF-Kansas City). At the average station, for every 1 minute of two women in a row you get more than one full hour of two men in a row.

calculation.output:
Mean station gap: 64.55%
Min gap: 58.16%
Max gap: 73.44%

ana_12.label: 24-hour listener experience: ~2 women, ~205 men back-to-back
ana_12.content: Recasting the data in listener-time: at the average station on a single 24-hour day, you would hear about 1.6 back-to-back pairs of women's songs and about 205 back-to-back pairs of men's songs, out of roughly 315 total songs. If you tuned in fresh and caught a back-to-back pair in your first hour, the odds are 99.5% it was two men. To hear two women in a row you would, on average, need to wait the better part of a workday.

calculation.output:
Mean per-day total songs per station: 315.3
Mean per-day b2b women per station: 1.60
Mean per-day b2b men per station: 204.93

data_table.description: Estimated per-day listener experience at the average station

caveats.content: Sample is 19–20 sampled days in 2022 (last Friday of each month + 7 release-day Fridays for women artists), not every day of the year. The release-day boost likely makes these numbers slightly more favourable to women than a uniformly random sample would.

Coverage is 29 stations in 16 large U.S. metro markets. Smaller markets, satellite radio, and streaming country playlists are not included; conclusions are about commercial broadcast country radio in major markets.
Race coding is by the dataset's authors (white / POC) at the artist level. Mixed-gender ensembles are tracked separately from women-only ensembles.

Two ownership labels appear due to capitalization differences ('COX' for the KKBQ-Houston entry vs 'Cox' for KCYY-San Antonio). They likely refer to the same parent company, but are reported as listed.
